  • Blueprints are approximations of an abstracted game. Their exploitability in the real game can’t be measured here.
  • Exact library flops use the blueprint’s ranges, sampled to 1,000 hands per side, and turns and rivers keep a single pot-sized bet. Two sizes there would need 5-12 GB per flop, more than the laptop spares.
  • Each spot covers 30 or 100 representative flops, weighted by the share of all 22,100 flops each stands for. There are 1,755 strategically different flops, so coverage is the largest gap.

Next #

Let the builder finish rolling out the second bet menu, then compare the main lines’ 30 flops the same way. A third flop size (33%, 66% or pot) follows if those flops support it.

item.title: A Figgie bot that counts cards and reads the market
item.description: An exact Bayesian card counter that trades Jane Street’s card game, live on figgie.com and in a Python simulator.
item.content:encoded:
Figgie is Jane Street’s card-trading game. Four players each get ten cards from a 40-card deck in which one suit is secretly the goal, then trade with each other for four minutes in an open market. Every goal card pays $10 at the bell, and the rest of the pot goes to whoever holds the most of them. This bot plays it, live on figgie.com against the site’s Hard bots and in a simulator against opponents written to beat it.

The full write-up tells the story version by version, including the ideas that lost money.

How it thinks #

  1. It counts cards exactly. There are only 12 possible decks, so it keeps the probability of each. Its own hand is the first evidence, and the tape adds hard facts: nobody can sell a card they don’t hold.
  2. It reads the market. High bids are votes for a suit. The cleanest tell is player by player: every Hard bot bids the goal suit up at some point, while a dead suit draws a big bid from only one of them. A bid counts only once it has stood on the book in two different seconds, so a flashed bid can’t steer it.
  3. It prices adverse selection. Early in a round, whoever buys from it probably knows more, so its offers are priced as if they do, and it never sells a card for less than the option of holding it.
  4. It values the majority bonus. Once it holds half the goal suit, the next card decides between a tie and a win, and it pays up for it.
  5. It learns from the table. An online Bayesian logistic regression learns which cheap offers resell within seconds, from every offer on the tape, and at each bell it updates how far to trust each market signal at that table.

Results #

Across 142 live rounds it made $6,958 in play money. Every live test since v3 has been profitable, and over the last 41 rounds (v11 to v13.3) it averaged $81 a round, ±$18 at 95% confidence, with 34 of 41 rounds in profit. The newest version opens its own tables and runs unattended: its first long session made $810 over 11 rounds at three tables.

Version Live rounds Per round ±95% What changed
v1 9 −$29.0 ±35 Exact card counting, naive market-making
v3 10 +$42.3 ±35 Won’t sell a card before the market reveals the goal
v8 10 +$33.5 ±34 Weighs whether every opponent bid a suit up
v10 10 +$60.3 ±34 Buys cheap dead cards and resells them, with a kill switch
v12 10 +$79.9 ±34 Learns which cheap offers resell, from the tape
v13 10 +$98.9 ±32 Learns which market signals to trust at a table
v13.3 11 +$73.6 ±37 Reacts to each quote at once; runs unattended

Ten rounds is a small sample: most single steps between versions are inside the noise, so decisions were made on paired simulations (the same deals for both versions) and replays of logged rounds, with live tests as the final check.

What it still gets wrong #

  • Colluders who know the goal beat it. Three of them take about $60 a round in the simulator whatever it believes, because they sell it dead cards and buy its goal cards.
  • Its opponents are bots, not people. figgie.com’s bots are predictable in ways people aren’t.
  • A better forecast didn’t pay. A model that read each opponent’s tells put more probability on the true goal and still lost $2 a round in simulation, because the bonus goes to whoever commits.

How it’s built #

The game engine, the probability model, a simulator with fifteen kinds of opponents and the analysis tools are about 4,400 lines of standard-library Python. A test bench, the arena, plays every change in paired sessions at 21 tables with separate seeds for tuning, choosing and reporting. The live bot is a 2,900-line userscript that carries a line-for-line JavaScript port into the page, and a harness checks that both versions compute the same probabilities and send the same orders.

It only trades at private tables where every other seat is a figgie.com bot, for play money, uses only what a player can see and places at most four orders a second.

item.title: A deal tracker for Coherent and AAOI that quotes every claim verbatim
item.description: A daily pipeline over filings, newsrooms, trade press and Chinese exchange disclosures, with a hand-curated layer of deals re-checked against its sources on every run.
item.content:encoded:
This is a commercial-intelligence database for two US makers of optical components for data centres: Coherent and Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI). It collects primary sources about them and their customers, suppliers and competitors, pulls out commercial events such as contracts, design wins and capacity changes, and writes a daily and a weekly report. The question behind it: how much can be established about these companies’ deals from public documents alone, with every claim tied to its evidence?

How it works #

  • Collection. SEC filings for both companies since 2016 and for 14 peers and DSP-chip vendors since 2021, plus SEC full-text search, XBRL financial data, company newsrooms, trade-press feeds, Texas construction-project filings for new fabs, federal awards, patents and the exchange disclosures of nine Chinese competitors. Every request checks robots.txt and per-host rate limits, and every raw response is stored with a checksum. Sources that block scripts or rule out automated access, such as the big newswires, LinkedIn and paywalled research, are listed with the reason and never requested.
  • Extraction. A gazetteer recognises companies, technologies and products, with date windows and guards: “coherent optics” is not the company, and Finisar folds into Coherent after the merger. Twenty sentence-level rules tag events. Boilerplate and risk-factor lists are filtered out, and a sentence already seen in an earlier document counts for less, so a press release mirrored in an 8-K is not news twice.
  • Scoring. Each event gets a 0–100 materiality score from the source’s tier, the type of event, the named counterparty and any stated dollar value relative to the company’s revenue. It is a ranking, not a forecast.
  • Curated layer. Deals, relationships, facilities, capacity statements, launches and industry developments are written by hand as records with verbatim quotes. Every quote is checked against the stored source text on each run, and any change creates a new version. An undisclosed customer is never named as fact: an identification is a separate record marked “inferred”, with its corroboration and a confidence level.
  • Monitoring. A scheduled job runs every morning. It collects new documents, re-verifies the curated layer, writes the reports and raises alerts for material items first seen since the previous run.

What it found #

The first build, on 12 November 2026, held 13,297 documents from 20 sources and 149 curated records, all of which passed verification. Some of what it documented:

  • One customer, two suppliers, one day. NVIDIA signed near-identical multi-year purchase agreements with Coherent and Lumentum on the same day in March 2026, each with a $2bn investment. Coherent rose 15.4% against a flat S&P 500 that day, so the deal was not expected.
  • An undisclosed customer, by arithmetic. Revenue linked to Amazon’s warrant was 26.4% of AAOI’s revenue in the first nine months of 2026, matching the 26% the 10-Q gives for AAOI’s second-largest customer. That makes Amazon very likely customer number two. It is an inference from matching numbers and is stored as one.
  • A disclosure in someone else’s filing. Coherent’s prepayment for indium-phosphide substrate capacity appears in its supplier AXT’s filing, not in Coherent’s own.
  • Filings that disagree with themselves. Two of AAOI’s 10-Ks each give two different figures for Microsoft’s share of revenue; the 2021 report says both 14.1% and 25.6%. The customer-concentration parser reconciles these sentences across filings and flags the conflict instead of silently picking one.

Limits #

  • The rule-based extraction aims for recall, so an event needs reading before it is relied on.
  • No consensus estimates are connected. The stock’s reaction around a disclosure stands in for “was it expected”, and that reaction mixes in everything else released that day.
  • Coherent does not file its customer or supply agreements as exhibits, so their terms are known only from press releases and 10-K summaries.
  • History is uneven. Coherent’s newsroom sitemap starts in December 2020, and most trade press is complete only from the start of collection.

How it’s built #

Python with SQLite, using WAL mode and FTS5 full-text search with BM25 ranking, plus requests, BeautifulSoup and pypdf for retrieval and text extraction. A command-line tool covers search, events, deals, company profiles, customer-concentration history and announcement-day returns, and exports plain CSV and Excel files. Twenty unit tests run without network access.

item.title: A Clash Royale win-probability engine, tested in a synthetic toy world
item.description: A research codebase for win probabilities, video-to-game-state reconstruction and an offline game-playing bot. No real game data has been used yet; everything runs on fictional cards.
item.content:encoded:
Clash Royale is a real-time card game in which two players spend elixir to deploy troops and spells and try to destroy each other’s towers. This project is a research codebase for it: a calibrated win-probability engine, game-state reconstruction from video, an analytics dashboard and a bot that plays offline.

No real Clash Royale data has been used yet. There was no API key, no sourced card statistics and no gameplay footage. Every model, metric and video so far comes from a synthetic toy world: 21 fictional cards, a toy simulator and scripted players, built to copy the game’s structure. The numbers below test the pipeline and the design choices in a world with known ground truth. They say nothing about accuracy in the real game.

What it does #

  • Data layer. A client for the official API, a crawler, a database that records where every row came from, and a card database that knows each card’s stats on any date, so balance patches enter as changed numbers. So far it has only run on fictional data.
  • Win probability. A pre-match model for two known decks, a prior that sharpens as the opponent’s cards are revealed one by one, and an in-game model that updates that prior from towers, elixir, the board and the opponent’s likely hand. Predictions are calibrated and explained with SHAP attributions (how much each group of inputs pushed the number).
  • Vision. Frames rendered from simulator states, each watermarked “SYNTHETIC”, are read back into game states (timer, tower HP, elixir, hand, units) and scored against the simulator’s ground truth. This tests the logic, not detectors on real footage.
  • Bot. Rollout-based search (beam search, a flat Monte Carlo search and one-step lookahead), in the toy simulator only. The game’s fair-play policy bans bots in real matches, so the code has no client interaction, screen tapping or network code.
  • Dashboard. A local web app with a matchup analyser, a match replay that charts the win probability and explains its swings, and a model report.

Results in the toy world #

The world has 600 fictional players and 12,000 matches over 60 simulated days, split by time into training, validation and test windows.

  • On 2,000 held-out matches, the pre-match model picks the winner 66% of the time (AUC 0.73, where 0.5 is a coin flip), against 53% for a baseline that only knows card levels and trophies.
  • In the first version of the world, in-game accuracy rose from about 62% in the first 30 seconds to 85% in the last 30 seconds of normal time. Tower state carried most of the signal.
  • A random train/test split would have overstated pre-match quality (log loss 0.573 against 0.612 on a split by time), so only time-split numbers are reported.
  • The largest single gain came from simulation: projecting tower damage eight seconds ahead improved the in-game model at every stage of the match.
  • Search-based bots beat the scripted players by a wide margin, with beam search strongest, at 20-100 ms a decision. Tuning a bot’s weights on 16-game evaluations overfit and made it worse in a fresh league.

What the review caught #

A technical review re-ran each idea on identical test rows, with confidence intervals that resample whole matches. It found that 8.1% of matches in the first world were near-idle because the scripted players could stall, and a second version of the world removed them. It also found that the opponent-elixir tracker was confidently wrong when plays were missed: its 95% intervals covered the truth only 20% of the time. Modelling missed detections explicitly raised that to 90%. Several ideas measured no gain and were dropped, including stage-by-stage recalibration and lagged history features.

Limits #

Real data is the whole gap. The in-game model needs real match timelines, which only screen recordings and trained detectors can supply, and the simulation feature needs a faithful game engine.

How it’s built #

Python throughout: SQLAlchemy and SQLite for the data, LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost and scikit-learn for the models, SHAP for explanations, OpenCV for the vision pipeline and FastAPI for the dashboard’s API. The dashboard itself is plain JavaScript with Chart.js.

item.title: Six tests of market contagion: no early warning, adaptive models win
item.description: A reproducible platform for how shocks spread across US stocks, rates, credit, currencies and commodities, with every claim labelled descriptive, predictive or causal.
item.content:encoded:
Contagion Lab is a research platform for how financial shocks spread across US stocks, sectors, banks, Treasury yields, credit, currencies, commodities and volatility indices. It asks six questions a risk manager would ask, and writes each answer from the computed numbers rather than from a verdict decided in advance.

How it works #

  • Data. 93 daily series from Yahoo Finance, FRED, Cboe and the Federal Reserve, aligned on NYSE trading days. The main cross-asset network has 15 series from April 2003, and the data run to November 2026.
  • Timing as data. Every series carries its closing time. Tokyo closes before New York opens and some prices are stale, so part of what looks like a shock spreading over several days is a series taking in the previous day’s US news late. That lag is measured for each series.
  • Clean inputs. Yahoo’s daily currency bars changed convention around 2011, so FX comes from the Fed’s noon rates; oil and gold futures are spliced into ETF prices to remove roll jumps and the negative oil print of April 2020.
  • Models. Correlation and partial-correlation networks, dynamic factors, Granger and VAR networks, Diebold-Yilmaz connectedness (the share of each asset’s forecast-error variance that comes from the others), tail dependence and CoVaR, copulas, hidden Markov regimes, change-point detection and DCC-GARCH.
  • Claim levels. Every result is labelled descriptive (co-movement only), predictive (lead-lag content, tested out of sample) or identified (causal under stated assumptions), and the report keeps them apart. Every out-of-sample routine sees data up to the previous day only.

What I found #

Question Answer
Does connectedness rise before crises? Not reliably: no consistent build-up before 7 bear-market peaks (placebo p 0.47; smallest corrected q 0.36). It rises during crises and adds nothing out of sample beyond VIX and realised volatility
Which assets transmit shocks? Equities in the standard sense, but about 90% of that is same-day co-movement. Lagged spillovers are 1–3% of connectedness and line up with series that react late
Which sectors are most rate-sensitive? Real estate, homebuilders and utilities on descriptive betas. FOMC days identify the S&P 500’s response, −0.98% per 10bp policy-driven rise in the 2-year yield, but only 3 of 18 sector responses precisely
Do dynamic networks improve stress tests? Yes. An exponentially weighted (EWMA) covariance cuts stress-day prediction error by 18% against a static network (t −3.9). Yet every model’s 90% intervals cover only 62–80% of stress-day moves
Are tail correlations more informative? Tail dependence is real, but correlations measured on past tail days forecast future ones no better than the full history
Does regime detection improve hedging? No. Hedging with Treasuries, gold and the dollar, an adaptive (DCC) hedge cuts S&P 500 variance by 24.7%; hedges built on a hidden Markov regime model cut it by about 6%, no better than a static hedge

The models that win the stress tests all weight recent data heavily, while covariances conditioned on past crises do worse. Crises differ: the stock-bond correlation had opposite signs in 2008–2020 and in 2022.

The regime model’s value is episodic. In the 2020 crash its hedge lost 22.7% against 33.4% unhedged. In the 2022 rate shock it stayed long Treasuries while stocks and bonds fell together, and lost 40.1% against 24.1% unhedged. That fits a high-volatility state learned from flight-to-quality crises: the model can tell that markets are stressed, but a hedge needs the current correlation, not that of past crises.

Limits #

  • Seven crisis onsets is a small sample, so a modest pre-crisis effect could be missed.
  • Long credit history relies on Moody’s Baa spread, which updates a day late relative to equities, because the free ICE BofA spreads go back only three years.
  • No model is well calibrated: every stress-test interval here is too narrow for real stress days.

How it’s built #

A Python package with a data pipeline, network and regime libraries, a stress-testing engine with seven covariance views, and portfolio-risk tools (value at risk, expected shortfall, Euler risk decomposition). 33 estimator tests run on simulated data. A report and a six-view D3 dashboard are generated from the same outputs. The public repository holds the code, figures, tables and report, but no market data.

item.title: Reading Axon’s government business from public procurement records
item.description: A traceable database of federal awards, city payments and council approvals, and an operating model built on it. The data explains demand, not quarterly surprises.
item.content:encoded:
Axon Enterprise sells TASER devices, body cameras and evidence-management software to police forces and other government agencies. Its customers buy in public, so much of its business leaves a paper trail: federal contract records, city payment ledgers and council agendas. I wanted to know how much of that business those records reveal, and whether they help forecast revenue.

How it works #

The pipeline collects procurement records naming Axon or its competitors, each traceable to its raw source:

  • Federal: USAspending contract records for FY2008–FY2026 (19,642 awards and 31,143 modifications), plus SAM.gov solicitations and sole-source notices.
  • State and local: payments in about 50 open-data checkbooks and New York City’s, co-op purchasing sales in Texas and Washington, and 4,905 council items from 202 city and county councils.
  • Context: the EFF’s Atlas of Surveillance (police technology deployments by vendor) and Axon’s own SEC filings.

The records hold four kinds of dollar figure, and they are never added together: federal obligations (money legally committed), ceilings on contract vehicles, council-approved values (usually multi-year maximums) and payments. None of them is treated as revenue.

63 federal awards matched FPDS, the federal system of record, field by field on dates, obligations and competition. Manual samples found reseller attribution right in 38 of 40 cases and 27 of 30 council approvals to be genuine Axon purchases. Each error became a rule with a regression test, from a medical-device brand that shares the Axon name to body-worn antennas that are not body cameras. Council attachments sit on hosts whose robots.txt blocks all crawlers, so terms and renewal dates come from each item’s full text via the Legistar API, with the supporting sentence kept verbatim.

What I found #

  • Federal orders are lumpy but rising. Direct obligations went from $19M in FY2020 to $101M in FY2023, dipped to $73M in FY2025 and reached $149M in FY2026.
  • Most federal money is not competed. 71% of Axon’s federal dollars were awarded without competition, and the median award drew one offer. When the Bureau of Prisons opened its body-camera and evidence contract to competition in 2026, Motorola won the $78M award from four offers.
  • Local spending tracks reported revenue. In the open-checkbook sample, payments to Axon grew 28% a year from 2019 to 2025, against Axon’s reported 31.5% for US revenue. Existing customers spend about 1.2 times as much each year, and 89% of paying governments pay again the next year.
  • The contested front is licence-plate readers. Flock Safety holds 88% of named deployments, and its council approvals rose from 0–6 a year in 2016–21 to 34–38 in 2023–24.
  • An expiry calendar dates 437 contracts and vehicles ending in 2026–2028, each with the basis for its date.

The operating model #

A quarterly model for FY2019–FY2030 forecasts revenue and gross profit by product line, in separate low, base and high cases. The procurement data sets the growth anchor for software and services (the same-customer spend ratio), the run-rates and odds of federal renewals, and range checks on US growth. Base revenue is $6.5B in FY2028 ($5.4B to $7.8B across the cases). The growth paths dominate: the three largest each swing FY2028 revenue by about $0.6B, while any one contract event moves it by about $50M at most.

Two tests came back negative. An installed-base refresh model could not be calibrated without unit counts and prices, so it was dropped. And in a 23-quarter backtest, no procurement indicator predicted quarterly revenue surprises: the data follows multi-year demand, not the quarter in which revenue lands.

A formula-driven Excel version, checked cell by cell against the Python engine, adds a discounted cash-flow valuation. Its base case gives about $186 a share, against a market price of $315 on 11 November 2026, and $21 to $632 across the low and high cases.

Limits #

  • State and local coverage is a sample of governments that publish their data, not a national total.
  • Seat counts and unit prices sit in those council attachments, which stay unread.
  • Reseller sales with generic descriptions such as “cameras” cannot be attributed to any vendor.

How it’s built #

Python and SQLite, with one HTTP client that checks robots.txt, throttles per host and caches every raw response with a timestamp and checksum, so re-runs reproduce the same figures offline.

item.title: Nine reinforcement-learning traders, and none beat buy and hold
item.description: A trading environment with realistic costs, nine RL algorithms, a full baseline suite and a holdout evaluated once. The controls work; the agents add nothing.
item.content:encoded:
Any reinforcement-learning (RL) agent can be made to produce a good backtest. The question here is whether RL adds anything over simple, well-understood strategies once execution is realistic and the evaluation is honest. On daily data the answer was no: none of nine algorithms beat simple strategies out of sample, and nothing, rule or agent, beat holding SPY on returns.

How it works #

  • The environment. An agent decides at the close and fills at the next open, paying a tick-size spread, slippage, square-root market impact, commission, a participation cap, financing and short borrow. Every baseline goes through the same environment and pays the same costs.
  • Nine algorithms, all in PyTorch: tabular Q-learning, DQN, Double DQN, A2C, PPO, SAC, TD3, Moody–Saffell recurrent RL and PPO-LSTM. Each was first checked on problems with known answers.
  • Controls before conclusions. Synthetic markets with a planted edge, a pure random walk, and an “oracle” feature that reveals the next day’s return.
  • Honest evaluation. Six walk-forward folds on SPY, a 2019–2026 holdout evaluated once with every access logged, seed ensembles with bootstrap intervals, and deflated Sharpe ratios that count all 72 strategies tried. The Sharpe ratio is annualised excess return over volatility.

What I found #

  • The controls pass. PPO, A2C and recurrent RL find planted edges (test Sharpe 0.64–1.19), no agent beats chance on a random walk, and all nine reach a Sharpe of 12–14 with the oracle, so the implementations work.
  • SPY, 2007–2018. The agents score 0.19–0.53 against buy and hold’s 0.41, with no significant difference, and all trail a 50/200-day moving-average trend filter (0.61). Across all 72 strategies, the best information ratio against buy and hold is −0.03. Higher Sharpe ratios came from holding less risk in 2008, not from earning more.
  • Holdout, 2019–2026. Buy and hold scores 0.77; the RL configurations 0.67 down to −0.52. The development ranking reversed (rank correlation −0.63): the best development agents were among the worst.
  • More assets did not help: on nine ETFs the best agent’s 0.52 trails minimum variance’s 1.09.

The lessons about method travel further than the null result:

  • Validation does not predict test. Across 162 runs, the validation Sharpe of the chosen checkpoint had almost no relation to the next two years’ test Sharpe, and training to the end beat validation-selected checkpoints for six of nine algorithms. A hyperparameter search bought nothing out of sample.
  • Leakage beats every algorithm. One feature built from a centred moving average, which sees ten days ahead, turns a random walk into a Sharpe of 6.9 and fools validation just as much.
  • Turnover is the hidden variable. High-turnover agents lose half their Sharpe by about $20 million of capital, even in SPY.
  • Reward hacking appears in mild forms. Drawdown penalties collapse exposure while the Sharpe ratio survives, and a risk stop without a penalty invites more risk.

Audit and limits #

An independent audit of the code found no look-ahead, but nine real problems in data, costs and statistics, such as fictitious futures roll jumps and hindsight in a stock list. All were fixed and earlier runs re-scored. Writing the report exposed one more: a policy that never trades had a Sharpe ratio made of rounding noise, which had steered the first hyperparameter search towards doing nothing. The metric was fixed and the search repeated.

The data is daily bars from a free source, with no intraday or order-book data, and the cost parameters are generic rather than broker quotes. With two or three seeds per configuration and twelve years of test data, differences below about 0.3 Sharpe cannot be resolved.

How it’s built #

A Python package with a vectorised numpy environment (about 17,000 steps a second per core), PyTorch agents, a baseline suite, Optuna search and a training dashboard. Every run records its config, seed, environment version and code fingerprint. 23 tests cover exact P&L accounting, execution timing, costs, short-sale bans and causality, including a check that catches four deliberately leaky features.

item.title: Netflix: the world is still switching, and the price assumes it has stopped
item.description: BUY with a 12-month target of $71, the probability-weighted DCF value. At $60.75 the market implies Netflix’s share of broadband homes outside the US & Canada falls from 34% to about 27% by 2035; the base case has it rising to 41%.
item.content:encoded:
Written for the Wharton Investment and Trading Group’s TMT committee (version 2, 17 November 2026). Research cutoff 17 November 2026; prices at the 16 November 2026 close; per-share figures after the 10-for-1 split of November 2025.

Snapshot
Recommendation BUY (12-month horizon)
Price (16-Nov-2026 close) $60.75
12-month price target $71 (the probability-weighted DCF value; +17.6%, against our 15% BUY hurdle)
Bear / Base / Bull $43 / $73 / $97 (the DCF value of each case)
Market cap / enterprise value $249B / $257B (4.11B basic shares; net debt $7.1B)
What would make us sell International member growth below ~3% a year for two years, or a 2027 US price increase that raises churn

Three thesis points

  1. The international switch to Netflix is a decade-long trend, and today’s price gives it no credit.
    • Only about a third of broadband homes outside the US & Canada pay for Netflix (34%), against about two thirds at home (63%).
    • International members grew 6–16% a year in 2025–26.
    • Our base case lifts international penetration to 41% by 2035. At $60.75 the market implies it falls to ~27%.
  2. Pricing power, not advertising, carries the US business, and live sports protect it.
    • The US & Canada region is nearly saturated, so its growth is price.
    • Live events are Netflix’s answer to the last reason people keep cable (sports and news). They cost ~5% of content spend and drive 6 of the 10 biggest sign-up days in five years.
    • A full-season sports package would need a ~9% price increase to pay for itself. Netflix’s “events, not seasons” approach is the right one.
  3. India is the biggest long-run opportunity and the smallest near-term number.
    • Members could reach ~50M by 2035 (from ~20M), but at ~$2.50 a month India stays under 2% of revenue.
    • Prices have not moved since 2023, and JioHotstar (IPL cricket, >300M subscriptions) owns sports.
    • India is an option on future pricing and a content factory, not a reason to own the stock this year.

Key catalysts:

  • Q4-26 results and the 2027 guide (~19–20 Jan 2027; options imply ±9.8%).
  • The FY26 engagement report (Q1-27).
  • The ad plan launching in 12 new countries (March 2027).
  • The next US price increase (implied ~Q2-27).
  • The NFL Week 18 game (9 Jan 2027) and the Women’s World Cup (Jun–Jul 2027).

Principal risks:

  • YouTube taking time from Netflix faster than prices can rise.
  • International price competition, India above all.
  • Currency (EMEA and LATAM are ~44% of revenue).
  • Sports-rights inflation if Netflix starts bidding for full seasons.
  • A higher cost of capital.

Exhibit A — What the Street expects vs. our base case

2026E Street 2026E Ours 2027E Street 2027E Ours 2028E Street 2028E Ours
Revenue ($B) 51.1 51.1 56.6 55.8 ~63.1¹ 60.5
Revenue growth 13.1% 13.2% 10.7% 9.2% ~11.5% 8.4%
Operating margin 31.5% (guide) 31.5% ~33.3%² 33.5% 36.1% (UBS) 34.7%
EPS ($) 3.58 (incl. fee) 3.08 ex fee 3.77 3.70 4.50 4.34
Paid members (M, year-end) 348–355 (JPM, Gugg) 352 — 372 382–402 392

Sources: Yahoo Finance consensus, 17-Nov-2026; ¹ July (pre-Q3) consensus; ² Evercore ISI, 16-Oct-2026; JPMorgan and Guggenheim member estimates (Oct-2026); the model’s Summary sheet. “Fee” is the $2.8B Warner Bros. termination fee booked in Q1-26.

What changed since version 1 (HOLD, $68, earlier the same day). The first model was detailed (~2,800 formulas). It treated the ad plan as a heavy drag on revenue per member, and it stacked a separate “AI threat” scenario on top of each operating case. We rebuilt it as a simple model you can audit in ten minutes: households × penetration × price, by region, with 19 dials. Four things changed the answer:

  1. International adoption is now explicit. Penetration rises from 34% to 41% of international broadband homes, giving 508M members by 2035 (version 1: 458M).
  2. The AI and competition risks sit inside one bear case (returns on new content fall to 15%, margins stay flat) instead of a separate 25%-probability dimension.
  3. Margins and US pricing follow the evidence more closely.
    • Content falls to 29% of revenue and other costs to 28% by 2035, a 43% margin. That is still a slower climb than the Street’s (UBS 41% by 2030, Oppenheimer 38.5%).
    • US & Canada revenue per member grows 5% a year, below the ~6% a year of 2019–26.
  4. The target is the DCF value itself. It is the probability-weighted value today, not rolled forward a year at the cost of equity.

The base value moved from $65 to $73 and the target from $68 to $71. Our caution on advertising stands: the model uses all-in revenue per member, which already nets out members trading down to the cheaper ad plan.

1. Executive summary #

Netflix has fallen 55% from its June-2025 high (Exhibit 1). The worry is attention: YouTube’s share of US TV time hit 15.8% in August 2026, twice Netflix’s 7.7%. The 2026 ad target was also cut, to ~$2.7B. Meanwhile the business keeps compounding:

  • 2026: revenue +13% to $51.1B, operating margin 31.5% (from 29.5%), free cash flow ~$12B.
  • Q3-26: a record $4.8B buyback, and churn improved globally and in the US after price increases.

Investors are arguing about the wrong market. In the US & Canada, Netflix is already in ~63% of broadband homes, so the US is a pricing story. Outside it, Netflix reaches only ~34% of broadband homes, and those homes are multiplying: India’s broadband base has roughly tripled since 2019, and Latin America and Southeast Asia are still wiring up. Three secular forces push more of those homes to Netflix:

  • Broadband and smart TVs, which set the size of the market.
  • The decline of pay-TV, which frees up entertainment budgets.
  • Netflix’s local-content machine, where non-English titles are now more than a third of viewing.

Our simple model turns this into numbers. Members grow from ~352M (2026) to ~508M (2035), revenue compounds at ~7.2% to $96B, and margins expand to 43% as content grows slower than revenue. Our DCF value is $71 per share: the probability-weighted value of the bear ($43), base ($73) and bull ($97) cases. That is our price target, 18% above the price. At $60.75 the market implies international penetration falls to ~27% by 2035, from 34% today. We think that is too pessimistic, so we rate the shares BUY.

2. The model in one page #

Each region has three steps. Revenue is the sum of the five regions.

Step What it means Where the number comes from
Households Homes with broadband in the region World Bank/ITU fixed broadband (2024), India from TRAI (2026), grown at sourced rates
× Penetration Share of those homes paying Netflix Today: broker member estimates ÷ households. 2035: dial
× Price (ARM) Revenue per member per month, subscription + ads Today: 2026 revenue ÷ members. Growth: dial

Costs are two lines, content and everything else, each a % of revenue moving to a 2035 dial. Cash flow nets out the extra cash content needs beyond what is expensed. The DCF uses a 9.87% WACC. The terminal value assumes 2.75% growth after 2035 and that Netflix must reinvest growth ÷ return on new investment of its profit to get it. The price target is the probability-weighted DCF value (25% bear, 50% base, 25% bull); it is not rolled forward. In the workbook each case has its own sheet with the same layout (no scenario switch), and the Summary sheet weights the three DCF values into the target.

The 19 dials (base case; bear / bull in the model)

Region Households 2026 → 2035 (M) Penetration 2026 → 2035 ARM 2026 ARM growth / yr Members 2035 (M) Revenue 2035 ($B)
US & Canada 155 → 167 63% → 66% (61–70%) $19.36 5.0% (2.5–6.0%) 110 39.4
EMEA 357 → 427 33% → 41% (36–47%) $12.09 3.0% (1.5–4.0%) 175 32.7
Latin America 136 → 170 46% → 52% (47–57%) $8.68 2.5% (0.5–4.0%) 88 11.3
Asia-Pacific ex-India 181 → 226 30% → 38% (32–44%) $8.93 1.5% (0–3.0%) 86 10.4
India 65 → 154 31% → 32% (26–38%) $2.45 2.5% (0–5.0%) 49 1.7
Netflix 894 → 1,143 39% → 44% $12.53 ~2.7% (mix) 508 95.6

Global dials:

  • Content cost: 29% of revenue by 2035 (35.3% today; bear 35%, bull 28%).
  • Other costs: 28% (33.2% today; bear 32%, bull 27%). Together they give a 43% operating margin in 2035, up from 31.5%.
  • Cash content spend / amortisation: 1.05x.
  • Tax: 17%.
  • Net capex: 0.6% of revenue.
  • WACC: 9.87%.
  • Terminal growth: 2.75% (bear 2.25%, bull 3.25%).
  • Return on new investment: 22% (bear 15%, bull 30%).
  • Buybacks: 4% of shares a year.

The penetration path is front-loaded, like most adoption curves: about 40% of the gap closes by 2028.

3. The international secular shift #

The evidence that the switch is still happening.

  • Members: EMEA grew from 101M (end-2024) to ~118M (end-2026E), LATAM from 53M to ~63M, and APAC from 58M to ~74M. That is 6–16% a year, far faster than the US & Canada (90M → ~97M).
  • Revenue (Q3-26, constant currency): APAC +15%, LATAM +12%, EMEA +9%. Brokers expect members to keep growing 4–8% a year in EMEA and LATAM and 8–14% in APAC through 2028 (JPM, Guggenheim).
  • Content: non-English titles are more than a third of viewing, against under 10% a decade ago. Local hits from Japan, Korea, Mexico, Denmark, the Netherlands and India travel across borders.
  • Headroom: brokers estimate Netflix has reached under 45% of the broadband homes it could serve and holds ~5% of global TV time (JPMorgan).

Why it continues.

  • Broadband keeps spreading. Fixed broadband subscriptions grew ~19% a year in India (2019–24) and ~3% a year in Latin America. Fibre and fixed-wireless are reaching homes that were mobile-only.
  • Pay-TV is shrinking outside the US too. India’s DTH paying base fell ~12% year on year, and Latin American pay-TV is flat at ~53M.
  • A cheap entry price. The ad plan (US $8.99, UK £7.99), mobile plans (India ₹149) and partner bundles (Flipkart in India, telcos elsewhere) lower the price barrier.
  • Scale economics. Netflix’s ~$20B content budget, spread over ~350M members, buys a local slate no national rival can match, and each hit can then travel abroad.

Why it might not.

  • Price. International ARM is a fraction of the US figure ($12 in EMEA, $9 in LATAM and APAC ex-India, $2.45 in India), and currency weakness erodes it in dollars.
  • Engagement. Hours per member fell from 2.2 to 1.6 a day between 2023 and 2026 (UBS), as Netflix added lighter viewers.
  • Local competition. Free YouTube is strong everywhere, and local sports-led platforms (JioHotstar, DAZN, Globoplay) compete hard.

Exhibit 2 shows each region today against our 2035 range.

4. Region by region: the key conflicts #

Region Growth driver Key conflict Our base dial
US & Canada Price increases every ~15 months; ad plan; live events Saturated (63% of broadband homes); YouTube takes TV time; each increase pushes members to the cheaper ad plan, and a US step above $20 for the standard plan is untested (2027 needs one: Mar-26 increase laps) Penetration 66%; ARM +5%/yr (2019–26: ~6%)
EMEA Under-penetrated south and east, Middle East and Africa; local hits Western Europe is mature (UK subscription streaming plateaued at ~70% of homes, Ofcom); local content quotas and levies; broadcasters now partner with rivals (Disney+ to carry Channel 4); EMEA was the first region to slow (+9% FXN) 41%; +3%/yr
Latin America Pay-TV decline; Globo partnership; local slate Currencies: local prices rise ~6–8% a year but USD revenue gains less; Brazil tax dispute (~$0.6B charge in 2025); piracy 52%; +2.5%/yr
Asia-Pacific ex-India SE Asia broadband; anime and K-drama, which Netflix exports globally Japan and Korea are well served by local platforms (U-Next, Tving/Wavve, Coupang Play); APAC ARM flat at ~$7.3 (brokers); price-sensitive SE Asia 38%; +1.5%/yr
India Broadband homes ~2.3x by 2035; local slate (view hours +24% in Q3-26); Flipkart bundle No price increase since 2023 (₹149–649); JioHotstar owns cricket (IPL) and has >300M subscriptions; YouTube free; Amazon Prime ~65M 32%; +2.5%/yr

The pattern is consistent. Where Netflix is saturated it grows through price, and where it is under-penetrated it grows through members at low prices. The international thesis is therefore a member thesis. It raises revenue less than member counts suggest: global ARM grows only ~2.7% a year in our base case, below the ~3.6% revenue-weighted average of the regions’ own ARM growth, because low-price regions grow fastest (Exhibit 3).

5. India: what happens next #

Today.

  • Netflix India’s revenue was ₹3,769 crore in FY25 (+32%; filing via press), roughly $0.5B a year, against ~20M members (sources range 15–25M).
  • In Q3-26 Netflix had its largest-ever quarter of Indian member additions, helped by a Flipkart loyalty bundle that gives a free mobile plan to frequent shoppers. India revenue grew ~18% in constant currency and view hours 24%.
  • Prices are unchanged since 2023 (₹149 mobile to ₹649 premium), so growth is all volume.

The structural picture.

  • The market is huge: ~200M TV homes, ~65M broadband homes (wired 47M plus fixed-wireless 18M, TRAI May-2026), 173M paid streaming subscriptions (Ormax).
  • It is also the world’s hardest to monetise. The leader, JioHotstar (Reliance and Disney’s merged platform), has more than 300M subscriptions built on IPL cricket at very low prices. YouTube is free, and piracy is common.
  • Netflix’s position is the premium global storytelling brand plus a growing local slate, sold through bundles.

Our view (Exhibit 4).

  • Members grow with broadband homes to ~49M by 2035 (bear 40M, bull 59M), but revenue reaches only ~$1.7B (bear $1.1B, bull $2.6B), under 2% of Netflix’s revenue.
  • India’s value is optionality. If incomes and connected-TV adoption lift ARM toward $5 (the bull path), India becomes a ~$3B business in the 2030s.
  • It is also a content source for the rest of Asia.
  • What would change our mind: a price increase that holds (bullish), or Netflix matching JioHotstar on price (bearish).

6. Live sports and the cable bundle #

US pay-TV has shrunk to about 62M homes (41M traditional plus 21M virtual, low-reliability 2026 estimate), from about 100M at its 2010–12 peak. MoffettNathanson sees a floor of about 58M “sports-viewing” homes. What keeps people paying ~$80–100 a month is live sports and news. The networks know it: ESPN launched a $29.99 direct-to-consumer service and FOX One $19.99 (both August 2025).

What Netflix is doing. It is buying events, not seasons:

  • NFL: Christmas Day, Thanksgiving Eve, a Week 1 game in Melbourne and a Week 18 game on 9 Jan 2027, extended through 2029-30.
  • WWE Raw: weekly, ~$5B over 10 years.
  • Baseball: MLB’s Home Run Derby and Opening Night (2026–28), and the World Baseball Classic in Japan (~¥15B; the most-watched programme ever on Netflix Japan).
  • Football and boxing: the Women’s World Cup in the US and Canada (2027 and 2031), plus boxing.

Management says live is ~5% of the content budget and ~1% of viewing hours. But live produced 6 of the 10 biggest sign-up days in five years, and in-game ad inventory sells out (NFL Christmas 2025 sold out more than four months ahead).

The economics (Exhibit 5). A full-season national package costs on the order of $2B a year. To pay that back from US & Canada members alone, Netflix would need either a $1.71 a month price increase on every member (+8.8%) or 10.8M extra members (+11%). If neither came through, the events would have to generate about $2.5B a year of advertising on their own.

Events capture the “can’t miss” value of sports at a fraction of a season’s cost. Full seasons would turn Netflix into a sports-rights bidder against Amazon, YouTube, ESPN and the networks, which is the business that made cable expensive.

News and daily sports. Netflix will not build news. The TF1 partnership in France (launched June 2026: five live channels, including news and sports, inside the Netflix app) shows how to aggregate the cable “glue” without paying for rights. Morgan Stanley estimates that hosting paid third-party channels such as FOX One at a ~15% take could add ~$1.2B of revenue for every 20% share of the ~$40B non-Netflix US premium streaming market. That is not in our base case; it is upside.

How it enters the model. Live sits inside content cost (29–35% of revenue). Its benefit sits in US & Canada penetration (63% → 66%) and pricing (+5%/yr). We do not add a separate sports revenue line, to avoid double counting.

7. What the sell-side and buy-side expect, and where we differ #

Sell-side.

  • 33 of 51 analysts rate the stock Buy, 16 Hold and 2 Sell. The mean target is $85 (median $82, range $57–126). Most cut targets in October as the 2027 debate intensified.
  • Consensus EPS is $3.77 for 2027 and $4.50 for 2028.
  • The bulls (JPM, MS, UBS, DB, Guggenheim, Evercore) argue double-digit revenue growth with modest engagement, a new content chief and sports upside.
  • The bears (Wells Fargo $57, HSBC, Needham, Barclays) argue falling hours per member, YouTube and single-digit 2027 growth.
  • Brokers model members at ~348–355M for 2026 and 382–402M for 2028. Nobody models households or penetration by region, and nobody puts a dollar value on India.

Buy-side (Exhibit 6).

  • The stock trades at 16x 2027 EPS and 19.9x trailing earnings, the 2nd percentile of its history.
  • In Q3-26, 13F filings show growth funds selling: Fidelity −49%, Wellington −75%, Baillie Gifford −46%.
  • Value and multi-manager funds bought: Harris/Oakmark +73%, GMO +32%, Pershing Square +18% to 15.4M shares, Two Sigma.
  • Short interest rose to 92M shares, and options imply ±9.8% for January.

Where we differ

Topic Sell-side Buy-side (as priced) Our view Implication
International growth Member growth 5–14% a year to 2028, no long-run view Price implies international penetration falls (34% → ~27%) Penetration rises to 41%, with members tracking broadband adoption +$12/share vs the market-implied path
Near-term growth ~11% in 2027–28 Single digits 9.2% (2027), 8.4% (2028): price increases lap, low-price regions grow fastest EPS slightly below the Street ($3.70 vs $3.77)
Advertising ~$4B in 2027, a growth engine Discredited by the cut Inside all-in ARM. Mostly a cheaper entry price, partly offset by trade-down Not a reason to own the stock on its own
Sports Upside to 2027 sentiment Cost risk Events are high-return; full seasons would need a ~9% price increase Supports US pricing power
Valuation 17–20x 2028 EPS Trough multiple Target = probability-weighted DCF value, $71 (base case $73) BUY (+18%)

8. Valuation #

DCF value: $71.44 per share, which is our price target (+17.6%, above our 15% BUY hurdle). Each case gets its own full DCF, and the three values are weighted 25/50/25. We do not roll the value forward (Exhibit 7).

Bear Base Bull Weighted
Probability 25% 50% 25%
Revenue growth, 2026–35 3.9% a year 7.2% 9.6%
Operating margin, 2035 33% 43% 45%
Return on new investment 15% 22% 30%
Enterprise value ($B) 183.8 310.4 408.3 303.2
Equity value ($B) 176.7 303.3 401.2 296.1
DCF value per share $42.62 $73.18 $96.79 $71.44
Upside vs $60.75 −30% +20% +59% +17.6%

Base case: terminal value is 59% of enterprise value, and the value implies 19.8x 2027E EPS. Net debt is $7.1B and diluted shares 4,145M.

Reverse DCF. Holding our other base assumptions, $60.75 implies 2035 international penetration about 14 points below our base: roughly 27%, well below today’s 34%. The market is pricing Netflix to lose share of broadband homes outside the US even as those homes multiply.

Sensitivities (Exhibit 8):

Change Value per share
International penetration ±5 points by 2035 ±$4.6
Revenue per member ±1 point of growth a year ±$5
WACC ±0.5 point (9.4% / 10.4%) $79 / $68
Content cost ±2 points of revenue ∓$3

Each line shifts the base-case value of $73.18. The same WACC move takes the price target to $77 / $66: at a 10.4% WACC the upside falls to +9% and the rating to HOLD.

Comparables and history. NFLX trades at 16.1x CY2027 consensus EPS, against 18.5x for ad platforms and 15.9x for media (Exhibit 9). Its trailing P/E of 19.9x compares with a five-year median of 39.9x (Exhibit 10). On our 2027E EPS of $3.70:

  • 20x → $74;
  • 16–24x → $59–89 (Exhibit 11).

9. Stock behaviour #

Earnings days. They carry ~28% of NFLX’s return variance on 1.6% of trading days. The average absolute reaction is 8.2%, and 28 of 44 were negative (Exhibit 12).

Between prints. The stock is not flat: inter-earnings volatility is ~36% a year, twice the S&P 500, and the median cycle ends 12% from where it began. Options offered no reliable edge after spreads. The full study is Does Netflix trade flat between earnings?

Implication. Build the position before or after the January print rather than through it, and size it for a ±10% event move.

11. Red team and what would change our mind #

  1. The bear has a point on engagement. Falling hours per member could eventually cap price increases. We hold the US & Canada at +5% a year, below the ~6% of 2019–26 and the ~7% of 2026.
  2. Our household data are rough. Broadband subscriptions include business lines, members are not households, and the India ratio is inflated by mobile-only plans. The level of penetration is approximate. Its direction and the headroom are robust.
  3. We are below the Street on 2027–28 EPS. The BUY rests on the long run. If 2027 guidance disappoints, the stock can fall first.
  4. The BUY clears our 15% hurdle by under 3 points. With a 41% margin in 2035 and US pricing at +4% a year (our first version-2 settings), the target would be $69 (+13%), a HOLD. The rating therefore depends on Netflix keeping its pricing cadence and lifting margins about 1.3 points a year, slower than the Street expects.

We would downgrade on:

  • two years of international member growth below ~3%;
  • a failed US price increase;
  • Netflix bidding for a full-season sports package without a matching price increase.

12. Conclusion #

Netflix is a global subscription utility for entertainment. It is in about two thirds of US & Canada broadband homes and about a third of the rest of the world’s, and it is cheaper per hour than any rival. The market has priced it as if international adoption were over. We think the switch from pay-TV and piracy to paid streaming has years to run outside the US, that live events protect US pricing at a fraction of cable’s cost, and that India is a long-dated option. BUY, 12-month target $71, the probability-weighted DCF value.

About the model #

The model is an Excel workbook in six sheets:

  • Summary: rating, DCF value by case, price target, reverse DCF, financial summary vs consensus, WACC × terminal-growth sensitivity, live-sports break-even and model checks (all pass).
  • Assumptions: every input, with the 19 dials in Bear / Base / Bull columns and the evidence for each.
  • Base Case, Bear Case, Bull Case: identical layouts running revenue build → income statement → free cash flow → DCF.
  • Reverse DCF: the base case with 2035 international penetration solved so that the value equals the share price.

There is no scenario switch: every case is calculated on its own sheet. The penetration, revenue-per-member and content sensitivities in this memo come from a Python version of the model that reproduces the workbook to the cent. The detailed version-1 model and memo are archived.

Facts, estimates and opinions.

  • Revenue, margins, cash flow, guidance and prices are reported or market data.
  • Members after 2024 are broker estimates.
  • Households are World Bank/ITU and TRAI data with our growth rates.
  • India subscribers and revenue come from press reports of filings.
  • All 2035 dials are our judgement, with the evidence noted beside each dial in the model.
